title: National Western Center is losing relationship with neighbors, auditor finds
summary: An auditor’s report finds the $1.6 billion redevelopment is being run with "little accountability."
content: An audit of the development of the National Western Center found that Denver is stewarding the $1.6 billion project with “little accountability.” City residents asked the Denver Auditor’s Office to look into Ballot Measure 2C — a 2015 measure that approved $778 million of tourism tax funding for improvements at the National Western Center and the Colorado Convention Center. As part of the measure, the city helped create the National Western Center Authority, which is responsible for the operations and management of the campus. After reviewing invoices, procedures and processes, auditors found issues with oversight practices, expense documentation and the campus’s finances. A man walks a dog through a construction zone off Washington Street in Globeville, as the National Western Center looms behind them. May 27, 2025. “If the city and the authority are not good stewards of this money, they risk eroding voter trust, wasting funds, and not fulfilling promises made to the communities most impacted by the National Western Center,” the auditor’s final report said . The report included over two dozen recommendations, with the city agreeing to implement almost all. Neighborhood tension Despite massive investment in the National Western Center, the auditor’s office found that the campus is unable to prove it is meeting its tourism and financial sustainability goals. The report said that city and campus staff have not set measurable goals and do not keep complete or reliable data on events, attendance and tax records. “As a result, the city does not know whether it is meeting the commitments it made to voters under the 2C ballot measure,” it said. A home on land owned by the GES Coalition’s Tierra Colectiva land trust is seen from a bus as the nonprofit takes Mayor Mike Johnston on a tour of their neighborhoods, as they try to lock down commitments from him on the future of the “triangle” site at the National Western Complex. March 2, 2024. The report also found that the city’s relationship with Globeville and Elyria-Swansea — the two neighborhoods closest to the campus — is deteriorating. The authority isn’t effectively keeping the community engaged and informed about development, the report found. The authority’s responsibilities include raising and overseeing funds to invest in the surrounding community. The authority does much of its community fundraising by asking visitors to “round up” their purchases, but the report says visitors are left confused as to what constitutes a tip to vendors versus a donation for the community. Neighborhood advocates agreed with the audit. “This audit is bringing to light issues that we’ve been asking about for several years,” said Shannon Hoffman, the project manager for the Globeville Elyria-Swansea Community Investment Fund. “The Riverfront,” which is not a park, on the edge of the National Western Campus along the South Platte River. Nov. 8, 2022. The National Western Center and the city government agreed to implement 27 of the 28 audit recommendations. However, the city and authority declined to implement policies and procedures for invoice review and approval. “Existing processes already address invoice review steps and guidance checklists,” a city response said. More than $1 billion has been committed to the National Western Center. Measure 2C was meant to fund multiple improvements on the Western Center campus, including land remediation, a new livestock and equestrian center, a new parking structure, and improved neighborhood connectivity. In the early 2010s, the National Western Center’s future in Denver was at risk. The campus was aging, and the National Western Stock Show’s stewards were telegraphing a potential move outside of the city. But the city and the state committed to rehabilitating the campus and turning it into a year-round attraction. Part of that commitment was the funding from the 2015 ballot measure. A parking lot in the National Western Complex’s “triangle” parcel where homes once stood. March 2, 2024. Redevelopment, however, has been slow-moving and expensive. The city has committed roughly $1.6 billion to the project, with the Denver City Council approving $800 million of additional tourism tax funding last year following tense community debates. Upcoming projects include completing the equestrian center, adding a 160-room hotel and repurposing a historic building in the coming years. Beyond that, the city and authority aim to redevelop “the Triangle,” 50 acres that could become housing, commercial space and possibly a new arena.
